subject: pathology
title: Pituitary and adrenal pathology: adenomas, Cushing, Conn and phaeochromocytoma

steps.tx: **Pituitary tumours** expand the sella and compress the optic chiasm, so patients develop **bitemporal hemianopia** from crossing nasal fibres. Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning tumour and causes galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea because prolactin suppresses gonadal function in patients. Growth hormone tumours cause acromegaly, ACTH tumours cause Cushing disease, while many gonadotroph tumours present only through mass effect. **Dopamine agonists** shrink prolactinomas, whereas most other symptomatic tumours require transsphenoidal surgical removal for cure.
steps.say: Pituitary tumours are sellar masses that compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal visual field loss characteristically. Prolactinoma is commonest because prolactin secreting tumours present early with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea in young women frequently. Dopamine agonist therapy is preferred because prolactinomas shrink without surgery in most treated patients.

steps.tx: **Acromegaly** develops from growth hormone excess and causes coarse facial features, prognathism, sweaty enlarged hands and carpal tunnel syndrome. Diagnosis requires high IGF-1 with **failed suppression on glucose testing** because normal growth hormone should suppress after glucose loading. **Cushing disease** results from a pituitary ACTH adenoma and causes central obesity, striae, hypertension and glucose intolerance over time. High dose dexamethasone suppression and petrosal sampling separate pituitary disease from ectopic ACTH and adrenal causes.
steps.say: Acromegaly is a disease where growth hormone excess enlarges jaw, hands and soft tissues over many years insidiously. Glucose suppression testing is diagnostic because normal pituitary tissue suppresses growth hormone after glucose loading in healthy people. Surgery helps clinicians remove the adenoma while medicines control hormone excess beforehand.

vis.caption: Clinical features of acromegaly and Cushing disease

steps.tx: **Pituitary apoplexy** occurs when haemorrhage or infarction strikes an adenoma and produces thunderclap headache with visual loss rapidly. Ophthalmoplegia and adrenal crisis develop because expanding blood compresses cavernous structures and ACTH secretion fails suddenly in patients. Resuscitation begins with **stress dose steroids** before urgent surgical decompression protects vision and pituitary function from permanent loss. **Craniopharyngioma** causes calcified cystic sellar masses in children with short stature, visual loss and diabetes insipidus.
steps.say: Pituitary apoplexy is an emergency where haemorrhage into an adenoma causes thunderclap headache and visual loss suddenly without warning. Steroid resuscitation is urgent because ACTH failure produces adrenal crisis alongside the expanding sellar haemorrhage compressing vision. Surgical decompression helps clinicians preserve sight when performed before optic damage becomes permanent.

steps.tx: Adrenal cortex tumours present according to the hormone they secrete in excess over normal physiological control mechanisms. **Conn syndrome** causes hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis because aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium continuously. Renin becomes suppressed while aldosterone stays high, and adrenal vein sampling lateralises secretion before surgery removes an adenoma. **Phaeochromocytoma** secretes catecholamines from medulla and requires alpha blockade before surgery because unopposed beta blockade can precipitate crisis.
steps.say: Conn syndrome is a disorder where aldosterone excess causes hypertension with potassium wasting and metabolic alkalosis persistently over time. Renin suppression helps clinicians distinguish primary aldosteronism from secondary activation driven by renal artery stenosis physiologically. Alpha blockade is essential because phaeochromocytoma surgery releases catecholamines that surge blood pressure dangerously.

steps.tx: This abdominal scan shows a round **adrenal adenoma** arising from the left adrenal gland beside the upper pole of kidney. The labels summarise **Conn syndrome** because hypertension, hypokalaemia and a low renin high aldosterone pattern accompany this lesion clinically. Adrenal vein sampling appears because imaging alone cannot prove which gland secretes aldosterone when bilateral adrenal changes coexist in patients. Spironolactone bridges blood pressure and potassium control while clinicians complete lateralisation before adrenalectomy cures unilateral disease.
steps.say: This scan shows an adrenal adenoma because a round mass arises from the left adrenal gland clearly beside kidney. Conn syndrome is suggested because hypertension accompanies hypokalaemia and suppressed renin in primary aldosteronism cases clinically. Vein sampling helps clinicians prove lateral secretion before surgeons remove only the responsible gland.
